prompt: A senior reviewer has left 19 comments on your PR across four days — two about a real null-handling bug, the rest about naming, file layout, and preferring map over a for loop. Your PR is blocking two other people and he's the only approver for that directory. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Do not capitulate and do not dig in. Applying all 19 teaches him this works and turns your next PR into the same week; refusing wholesale means rejecting the two comments that were correct and turning a code disagreement into a personal standoff with the one person who can approve you. Instead, classify explicitly and reply once rather than 19 times: take the bug and any style points that match an existing written convention, then say plainly that the rest are preference — 'I do not think we have a convention for loop-versus-map or the file split, and I would rather not settle it in this PR since it is blocking two people. Can we take those to the style guide?' That is not a compromise for the sake of peace, it is the correct classification: without a convention, insisting is imposing taste using the leverage of an approval button. If he still blocks, escalate the process rather than the code — ask your lead whether single-owner directories should require a second approver, so no one person can hold a queue. What you avoid entirely is arguing about whether map is better, because that argument has no ending.

prompt: What is the actual standard for approving a code review?
answer_markdown: Google's engineering practices state it precisely: approve once the change definitely improves the overall code health of the system, even if it is not perfect. There is no perfect code, only better code. This single line resolves most standoffs, because most standoffs come from a reviewer comparing the PR against an ideal that does not exist rather than against the code currently in main. The question is not 'is this the best possible implementation?' but 'is the codebase better with this than without it?' The complementary principle is speed: reviews have a clock, and Google explicitly optimises for how fast a team ships together rather than how correct any individual review is. Every day a PR sits blocked, the author context-switches away, the branch drifts, and the merge gets riskier — so a review that is 10% better but four days slower is usually a net loss. This is also why reviewers are encouraged to approve while leaving unresolved non-blocking comments.

prompt: Why does labelling review comments with prefixes like 'Nit:' matter so much?
answer_markdown: Because without labels, every comment reads as mandatory. A reviewer leaves eight minor suggestions and one real issue; the author sees nine blockers and either spends a day on all of them or gets defensive about the whole set. Google's guide recommends prefixes precisely for this: 'Nit:' for minor details the author can take or leave, 'Optional:' or 'Consider:' for suggestions worth thinking about, and 'FYI:' for context requiring no action now. Anything unlabelled is understood to need addressing. Adopting this convention eliminates roughly half of all review standoffs at zero cost, because most of them were never real disagreements — they were a mismatch between how strongly the reviewer meant something and how strongly the author read it. It also makes genuine blocking comments land harder, since they now stand out rather than sitting in a wall of equally-weighted text.

prompt: You're reviewing a PR that builds a SQL query by string concatenation with user input. It isn't exploitable today because an upstream gateway strips quotes — but that gateway belongs to another team, isn't documented as a security control, and one team is discussing replacing it. The author says it's out of scope and the release is Friday. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Refuse the false binary between blocking the release and letting it go, because that is the actual test here. The danger is not today's exploitability — it is that the safety is accidental and undocumented, so the team that eventually replaces the gateway has no way to know they are removing a security control. That is exactly how injection vulnerabilities appear months later with nobody having made an identifiable mistake. First, check whether parameterising the query is a ten-minute change, because it very often is and the entire conflict evaporates. If it genuinely is not, you can accept the Friday schedule and still kill the ambiguity: write the risk down where the gateway team will actually see it, put it in the release notes and the security channel, and attach a named owner and a date. You have owned the risk by making it visible, which nobody else was willing to do and which costs the schedule nothing. Interviewers use this scenario because the real subject is diffusion of responsibility rather than SQL — two senior people said 'it is fine', and the question is whether you accept that as a resolution.

prompt: You're the reviewer. A newer engineer's 700-line PR works and has tests, but puts business logic in the HTTP handler — a pattern your team retired a year ago. He says it's tested, the deadline is Friday, and refactoring is out of scope. Do you block?
answer_markdown: Apply the actual standard first: is the codebase better with this than without it? If the logic is correct and tested, quite possibly yes, and blocking would be the wrong call. But approving and letting it rot are not the same thing — approve with a written follow-up ticket that has his name and a sprint on it. Crucially, explain why the pattern was retired using the concrete incident it caused rather than the principle, because 'we have a convention' persuades nobody while 'this exact structure caused the duplicate-validation incident in March' persuades most people. If the logic is not adequately tested, or it sits on a path where the duplication risk becomes a security or money issue, then it does block and you say so with the specific failure case. The distinction interviewers listen for is whether your block is anchored to a concrete consequence or to a preference wearing the clothes of a standard.

prompt: How do you review a junior engineer's code differently?
answer_markdown: The goal shifts from producing a better diff to producing a better engineer, which changes three things. Explain the why behind every substantive comment, since a correction without reasoning teaches a rule they will misapply in a slightly different context next month. Label severity clearly, because a junior engineer cannot tell your nit from your blocker and will treat all of it as failure — which is both demoralising and slow. And resist rewriting their PR in comments: handing over the finished solution is faster for you and removes the learning entirely, so point at the problem and let them find the fix. Two things do not change: correctness and security still block, because lowering the bar is not kindness and shipping their bug helps nobody. It is also worth being explicit about what is good in the PR, since junior engineers reading a list of 12 corrections have no way to calibrate whether that means the work was poor or completely normal.
